problem: Given that $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find $L{u(t-5)({t}^{2}+4t+1)},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}={e}^{-as}\,L{g(t+a)},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L{u(t-5)({t}^{2}+4t+1)}.
$$

Therefore, $a=5,$ and we have 

$$
L{u(t-5)\,g(t)}={e}^{-5s}\,L{g(t+5)},
$$

where $g(t)={t}^{2}+4t+1.$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+5) & =(t+5)^{2}+4(t+5)+1 \\  & ={t}^{2}+10t+25\,+\,4t+20\,+\,1 \\  & ={t}^{2}+14t+46.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ and $L{1}=\frac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+5)} & =L{{t}^{2}+14t+46} \\  & =L{{t}^{2}}+14L{t}+46L{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+14\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+46\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{14}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{46}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-5)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-5s}\,L{g(t+5)} \\  & ={e}^{-5s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{14}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{46}{s}).\end{aligned}
$$
